title: Trudie Styler Talks Journey To Directing ‘Up Against It’ & ‘The Reception’ Back-To-Back: “I’m In A Happy Place”
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie WTFilms Boards Italian Alps-Set Comedy-Thriller ‘The Dregs’ With Maddie Phillips & Stephen Lang – AFM Tinto Brass Dies: Italian ‘Caligula’ Director Was 93 Pierfrancesco Favino First Look In Marco Bellocchio’s Sergio Marchionne Bio-Pic ‘Falcon’ Unveiled – AFM View All November 4, 2026 7:29am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Trudie Styler on the London Underground with cinematographer Dante Spinotti during the shoot of Up Against It Andrew Cooper Trudie Styler arrives at the London offices of Maven Screen Media , her joint production company with Celine Rattray , bearing gifts: bottles of organic extra virgin olive oil. Featuring Styler and husband Sting ’s names on the label, they are the last of a batch made from the 2025 olive harvest at Villa Il Palagio, their beloved 16th Century estate in Tuscany. She is not here to talk about her long love affair with Italy, however, but rather back-to-back directorial feature film credits Up Against It and The Reception as well as her and Rattray’s commitment to championing female-driven storytelling. Related Stories News Jean-Claude Van Damme Returning To Martial Arts Roots In Yakuza Action Pic 'Katana' For Jeremy Zag & The Veterans -- AFM News Chris Jericho To Star In Creature Horror 'I Am The Teeth', Epic Launches Sales For AFM London-set romantic comedy Up Against It stars Antonio Banderas and Eva Birthistle as warring divorced couple Alvaro and Saffron, who are forced to reconnect when their only daughter Rose is struck down with cancer, an illness she had previously battled as an infant but has no memory of. It received a buzzy world premiere in Toronto. Watch on Deadline The Reception , revolving around a chaotic wedding party and featuring Jeff Daniels, Guy Pearce, Sabrina Impacciatore in the cast , is on the cusp of shooting in Scotland when this interview takes place, with cameras now rolling since late October. The features, being sold by Beta Cinema at the upcoming AFM , mark the latest chapter in a producing and directing career that began in the early 1990s when then actress Styler came to the conclusion that combining motherhood and repertory theatre or being on set was going to be a tall order, especially with Sting on the road touring. “I decided to give acting a pause,” she says, revealing that she called Oscar-winning Chariots of Fire producer David Putnam for advice. “I said, ‘Could we have a meeting, because I want to know something about being a producer, and if I’ve got it in me to be one, and if you think I’ve got it in me to be one’,” she recounts. “He was my great mentor in how to be a producer and getting IP… he described it as putting pans on stoves,” she says. “It wasn’t a bad concept… it was sort of like when there’s a bit of heat around one project, keep the others simmering, but really go all in for the one that is showing some heat.” Her first producer credit was 1993 documentary Boys from Brazil , sparked by Styler seeing Brazilian transvestites working as prostitutes in the Bois de Boulogne in Paris and then wondering about their back stories. She tapped John-Paul Davidson to direct. The pair met during a trip to the Amazon in the early days of the Rainforest Fund which Styler co-founded in 1988 with Sting to protect rainforests and their indigenous people. The resulting work would air as part of the BBC’s now defunct documentary Under the Sun strand. “It got like about 5.5 million people, which I was told was a good number, although it I got castigated by the fourth estate for making something in such poor taste,” says Styler. Davidson would go on to direct and produce the travel shows of Micheal Palin and Stephen Fry, while the fund has since raised more than $45 million for 300 indigenous driven projects across three continents. Her next project Moving The Mountain , was directed by Michael Apted (then fresh off 35 Up ) and took its title and cue from a book by exiled Chinese student leader Li Lu chronicling China’s 1989 pro-democracy protests and their brutal ending with the Tiananmen Square Massacre. He had been introduced to Styler by a friend shortly after his arrival in the U.S. in late 1989 after escaping China where he was wanted by the authorities. “I met him that winter and he’s been in my life ever since,” recounts Styler. “Now he has a big hedge fund company.” She enlisted Apted as a director after bumping into him on a flight on the way to New Orleans to join Sting in the city. “I said, ‘Oh, coincidence!’ And he said, ‘No, I’ve actually come to see your husband about a project’… I said, ‘Ah well, can I talk to you about my project’,” she recounts. Styler remains banned from China to this day due to the film, which played a raft of festivals including the Berlinale and won an IDA award. She would go on to produce a dozen documentary and fiction features under her Xingu Films banner, named after Xingu Park in Brazil, before going on to launch Maven with Rattray in 2011. Styler also earned kudos for her championing of emerging directors, with Xingu Films getting behind Guy Ritchie ’s 1998 breakout first feature Lock Stock and Two Smoking Barrels and follow-up Snatch (2000), as well as Duncan Jones’ Bafta-winning debut Moon (2009), for which she was also Bafta nominated, among others. She recalls being approached by Ritchie’s then rookie producer Matthew Vaughn , who knocked on the door of her home out of the blue. “Matthew had the native wit and charm and the brain to be able to manifest pretty much what he wanted. He said, ‘I want you to meet Guy. He wants to meet you. By the way, you know his father’, and I was like ‘I do?’” She discovered that Guy Ritchie’s father is John Ritchie, the advertising exec known for producing the iconic “Happiness a cigar called Hamlet” ads, who she had convinced to create a campaign for the Rainforest Fund. “When I met Guy, he asked, ‘So what did you think of my script?’ I replied, ‘Even if I thought it was really stupid, I would have done this to help you because your dad helped me’,” recalls Styler, suggesting that what Vaughn and Ritchie lacked in experience they made up for in chutzpah. “It was a seminal moment… those young bloods were going to do it no matter what.” Xingu’s filmography also includes Styler’s feature directorial credit on the 2002 documentary Sweatbox , co-directed with Davidson, going behind the scenes at the Walt Disney studios and the making of the animation The Emperor’s New Groove at Disney, in which Sting was involved as chief songwriter. Styler would break into fiction feature directing in 2018 with Freak Show, an adaptation of James St James’ best-selling novel, starring Bette Midler and Alex Lawther, before returning to documentary in 2023 with Posso Entrare? An Ode To Naples . Up Against It Up Against It Maven Screen Media She continues to tap into her process as a documentary producer and director for her fiction work. For Up Against It , she spent time with NHS oncologists, notably at the Royal Marsden Hospital in London, in preparation for the film, which hinges around the fact that the best shot at survival for Alvaro and Saffron’s daughter Rose is the conception via IVF of a so-called “saviour sibling” with matching T-cells. While the premise sounds dark, the film is not, with Styler bringing a celebration of life; love and moving on, while holding on, to the big screen, reminiscent of Working Title classics such as Love Actually or Four Weddings and a Funeral but more complex. “TIFF was sort of amazing because I wasn’t prepared to have the applause, and people weeping, and also really roaring with laughter… In Up Against it , you do laugh as much as you’re touched and moved… that’s why I love cinema as a shared experience,” she says. Styler directs from a screenplay by Camille Griffen, based on an original story by Chloe King who wrote a first draft after being inspired by a segment on the NBC’s Today Show. Citing her research and discussions with oncologists, Styler says that around four saviour siblings were created in Europe last year but that the practice is being superseded by developments in paediatric oncology and CAR T-cell therapy, which uses a patient’s own white blood cells to fight cancer “I didn’t connect with it through the cancer story as much as that of the couple,” reveals Styler. “The couple split up because of Rose’s cancer. It seemed counterintuitive that you would break up when your child was in desperate need of you both, but then I spoke to oncologists who said that the path to a cure amongst families who have got a long cancer protocol in their lives, often requiring the mum to stay in hospital with the child, can put an enormous strain on the marriage.” Although the story was born out of a U.S. news item, Styler opted to transpose it to the UK where she has a better grasp of the health system. “I don’t know enough about it to get into the weeds of what universal medical care is there, but I do know a lot about the NHS, so I thought I’m just on better ground and safer ground,” she says, With two sisters who worked as nurses, one specialized in intensive care for babies, and the other in women’s health, Styler also has a deep respect for the staff throughout the NHS. “They’re not paid that well. They do many, many more hours a week than many other professions do… I felt that in the movie it was important to really include them,” she says. Styler adds it was also a joy to bring London to life on the big screen, describing the film as a love letter to the city, where she was based in the early years of her career as an actress. “I wanted it to look beautiful and diverse… it’s full of so many nations. And at its best, I think it’s a glorious city,” she says. “Because I don’t live here all the time now, I think I have a great nostalgia for it, and all it gave me when I was 18, 19, and I started to live my life as an actor, and that’s all I’d ever wanted to be.” “Through my kind of rose-tinted eyes, it’s the city that really gave me the love of arts that I have. I remember going to see Ian McKellen and Judi Dench in their Macbeth at the Donmar Warehouse and how brilliant and simple it was,” she continues. “My agent at the time, Elspeth Cochrane, was Ian’s agent. She managed to purloin me a ticket and when I saw that, ‘I was like, oh God, I really want to be at the RSC and do this.” The cast and crew for Up Against It taps into Styler’s network built over her 50-year career and life on the celebrity circuit with Sting. Antonio Banderas, Trudie Styler and Úrsula Corberó on set of Up Against It “I knew Antonio in the 1990s when he was married to Melanie [Griffith]. Then for a long time, our paths did not cross. I was living in New York, and he came to live in England for a bit,” she says of her connection with Banderas. “I’d been thinking who could play Alvaro because he’s not to everybody’s taste with his sexist remarks… somehow Banderas is one of those transcendent actors in that whatever he does, he remains lovable.” She recounts how a month after she sent the screenplay to his agent Manny Nunez, the actor requested a Zoom call in which he said he loved the part but requested one tweak. “He said, ‘I really love the script, but what I cannot be is a barrister called Peter.’ I said, ‘Of course, we will tailor make it to you,” she recalls, with Peter then becoming larger-than-life conductor Alvaro. Further cast include Úrsula Corberó ( Money Heist ) and Arinzé Kene ( The Pass, Lee ), as Alvaro and Saffron’s new partners, who become unwitting peacekeepers in the IVF process overseen by the real-life Human Embryology Authority, as well as Forest Whitaker, as NHS oncologist Doctor Augustus Abara, with Richard E. Grant, Mickey Sumner and Selana Tan also putting in appearances. Eden Hamilton ( The Railway Children Return ) plays Rose. Styler’s connections with Whitaker go back to 2013, when she was a coproducer on Christmas musical A Black Nativity , in which he co-starred alongside Angela Bassett and Jennifer Hudson, with the film shooting on location in New York’s Saint John the Divine cathedral. When Whitaker revealed he was not happy with his hotel, Styler invited him to stay at her New York apartment instead. “He said, ‘I never do that kind of thing.’ I said, ‘Well, the offer’s there.’ Later in the day, he asked, “Are you serious about me coming to stay at your apartment? I’d be really quiet.” I said, ‘Forest, it’s not a small apartment. There’s plenty of room’. My kids had gone to college, or they were working elsewhere… and Sting was on the road. I said, ‘It would be lovely to have your company’. We’ve called each other roomie ever since,” she recounts. After accepting the Up Against It role, Whitaker requested time with an oncologist for a briefing on Rose’s treatment to understand the real-life protocols around treating cancer. Styler’s award-winning crew, featuring editor Walter Fasano ( Call Me By Your Name ), Dante Spinotti ( Heat, L.A. Confidential ) and late multi-Oscar nominated Ghandi and Blue Planet composer George Fenton, is also the fruit of long connections. She has known Spinotti since the 1980s, working with him on films such as Mario Orfini’s Cinecittà-shot 1988 film Fair Game ( Mamba), in which she starred as a woman locked in an apartment with a deadly snake by her deranged computer scientist husband. He previously worked on Freak Show and Posso Entrare? and is also the cinematographer for The Reception . The interview takes place just days after Fenton’s unexpected death at age 76 in early October . Styler is caught off guard by the mention of his name and looks visibly pained by the thought of his passing, with the interview pausing momentarily. Styler, who is still reeling from his death, explains her friendship with Fenton goes back to a 1978 theatrical production of Hamlet at the Belgrade Theatre in Coventry in which she played Ophelia and he oversaw the music. “I was 23… He wrote my songs for Ophelia and through the years we just sort of ran into each other, and then this year I had nine months with him, composing that very beautiful score, seeing so much of him, and it’s like we recaptured those days in 1978, I think it was just before he did Gandhi .” “Spending those nine months with him was a sheer pleasure and also did a lot for my confidence, with him encouraging me and saying, ‘When you played Ophelia, I came to your first night. I thought it was a really stunning performance, and now you’re a director. You go on and direct as much as you want because you’re good.’” Maven & Backing Female Driven Storytelling Producer Piers Tempest, Trudie Styler and Celine Rattray at the TIFF Up Against It premiere Getty Images While revelling in her time behind the camera, Styler remains committed to Screen Media, her joint female focused banner with Rattray. Launched in New York in 2011, with offices in London, the company moved its main base to the UK capital in 2025. When Rattray first approached Styler in New York with the idea of working together, she had been mulling a move back into acting despite the then recent success of Moon. “She said, ‘Well, have a think about it’, and I said, ‘If we do it, it’s going to be something that’s niche and focuses on something missing in the film industry… what’s missing?’ We both look at each other and go, ‘Us?’” “Seventeen years later, here we are, making films that have pushed the needle on women in film above and below the line, and we’re very proud of what we’ve done.” The slate to date has included Andrea Arnold’s American Honey (2016) as well as Sundance prizes winners Novitiate by Maggie Betts and The Kindergarten Teacher by Sara Colangelo, with more recent credits including Scarlett Johansson’s Cannes-selected Eleanor The Great, Gurinder Chadha’s Christmas Karma , and Katie Holmes’ romantic comedy Happy Hours , which debuted in Tribeca in June. Men are not excluded with the company also getting pictures such as Guy Nattiv’s’s Skin (2018) and Mark Meyers’ Human Capital (2019). Styler cites figures collated by the Center for the Study of Women In Television and Film for the top 100 grossing U.S. films of 2025 showing that women accounted for 26% of producers, 20% of editors, 20% of writers and 11% of directors. “Since we’ve been more based in the UK, 90% of our films have been female directed,” she says proudly, highlighting the contrast. Additionally, 80% of Maven’s films since 2020 have had women in the leading role, while 70% were written by women. Styler acknowledges that it remains an uphill battle for women to achieve gender parity in the film and TV industries, says she remains optimistic for the future. “I do feel that the demographics are behind us. When I look at my grandchildren, we’ve got eight. I see that they are incredibly well informed, and they are no pushovers. And I do think it will get keep getting better and that storytelling will be more female driven,” she says. “I have to think like that because the alternative is to give up and retire and swing in a hammock or something, but I don’t have that in me. I’ve got lots of energy, and I love doing what I’m doing. I’m a grandmother, and I’m 72… I feel it’s my time to do what I want, and I’m really not afraid of saying what I think to anybody about this situation.” “Celine and I will continue to push on female-driven stories written by women, with women cinematographers… and wherever we can populate the films with diversity and women we will do it because the industry needs it and the world needs it. We need narratives that are more balanced. Otherwise, we are telling so many male action movies that really don’t have a beating heart.” On her own personal journey as a director, she says it is too early to say what comes next after Up Against It and The Reception , but admits she is in her element right now. “I don’t know now how many more films I’ll direct. Antonio said to me, ‘You seem so peaceful when you’re directing, the set’s so quiet, you never raise your voice.’ It’s because I’m actually in a happy place with myself and I’m so grateful to all these collaborators that are part of this.” Antonio Banderas, Eva Birthistle and Trudie Styler on the set of Up Against It Andrew Cooper Bass & Raman In Dead Heat For Mayor As Counting Continues Elected California Governor In Rout Of Ex-Fox News Host Steve Hilton Jean-Claude Van Damme Returns To Martial Arts Roots In Yakuza Action Pic Sky-ITV: Competition Bodies Get Greenlight To Probe $2.2B Deal Read More About: Comments

title: Paris Creator Week Aims to Become the Cannes of the Creator Economy as New Study Forecasts $1.2 Trillion Global Market
full_text: × Breaking News Becerra Wins California Governor; Democrats Take the House and Senate Nov 4, 2026 7:26am PT Paris Creator Week Aims to Become the Cannes of the Creator Economy as New Study Forecasts $1.2 Trillion Global Market A study unveiled today at the event revealed that the global creator economy is on track to reach $217.3 billion in 2026, with France emerging as major hub. By Elsa Keslassy Plus Icon Elsa Keslassy International Correspondent @elsakeslassy Latest Paris Creator Week Aims to Become the Cannes of the Creator Economy as New Study Forecasts $1.2 Trillion Global Market 1 hour ago Dominic West, John Cleese, Portia de Rossi Join Jeff Daniels in Trudie Styler’s Comedy ‘The Reception’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago Cannes Chief Thierry Fremaux Hails French Film Model as CNC Head Gaëtan Bruel Vows to Fight for Its Future at 80th Anniversary 6 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Marc Lesage-Moretti Paris Creator Week is doubling in size this year, drawing 8,000 industry professionals and top executives from YouTube, Twitch, LinkedIn and traditional media giants including Banijay and Mediawan. The gathering kicks off today at the Halle de la Villette where a new study is being unveiled, revealing that the global creator economy is on track to reach $217.3 billion in 2026, marking a 26.2% year-on-year increase. The market, which has nearly tripled in size over the last five years, is projected to reach a staggering $1.22 trillion by 2033. Related Stories 'Ellen DeGeneres Show' EP Matthew Wright Dies at 52 in 'Unfathomable Tragedy'; DeGeneres Shares Tearful Video Calling Him the 'Glue to Our Family' France has emerged as a major international hub for the booming creator economy which will reach $10.1 billion locally this year, up 23.7% from 2025. It could more than double to $24.3 billion by 2030, per the study. That makes France the world’s seventh-largest creator economy and the third-largest in Europe, behind the U.K. and Germany. The sector already accounts for 227,000 full-time equivalent jobs in France. Marc Lesage-Moretti, a former Goldman Sachs vice president turned content creator, known online as Jokariz, who co-founded Paris Creator Week in 2024, says the findings underscore a dramatic shift in an industry which took time to be taken seriously. “In the United States, everyone was talking about the creator economy, but when I started using that term in France three years ago, people looked at me as though I was speaking Chinese to them,” Lesage-Moretti tells Variety in a zoom interview a few days before the start of the event. “They would say, ‘Oh, the creator economy? You mean 14-year-old kids making entertainment videos in their bedrooms on YouTube?’” “People hadn’t yet understood how much this industry was becoming professionalized,” he says, citing HugoDécrypte, the popular French digital news outlet, which now employs around 40 people, including journalists and human resources staff. The huge expansion of the Paris Creator Week this year underscores how the general perception has evolved. It’s grown from 4,000 participants last year to an expected 8,000 this year, while its exhibition space has increased fivefold, from 200 to 1,000 square meters. YouTube alone is taking a 100-square-meter stand, Lesage-Moretti points out. The event is also becoming increasingly international, with overseas attendees accounting for 30% of participants. Global platforms including YouTube, Twitch, LinkedIn, Spotify and SoundCloud are sending senior executives, while traditional entertainment groups are joining discussions about the future of content creation, distribution and monetization. “The idea is to create the VivaTech of the creator economy,” says Lesage-Moretti, referring to the major Paris technology conference. Unlike consumer-facing creator conventions, Paris Creator Week is positioning itself as a B2B gathering where creators, media execs, platforms, brands, agencies and investors can explore partnerships and new business models. The event’s growing appeal also reflects a major shift in advertising spending. According to the study, sponsorships and commercial partnerships now account for 49.8% of the global creator economy, followed by advertising on creator content at 22.7% and paid subscriptions at 13.8%. Advertisers are expected to contribute $172.8 billion to the sector in 2026, representing 79.5% of total spending, while creators themselves receive an estimated $92.6 billion, or 42.6% of the overall market. “Commercial partnerships are the main driver of growth,” Lesage says. “Brands that traditionally invested their money in other media or advertising channels are redirecting those budgets toward content creators.” “And we’re not just talking about luxury brands. We’re talking about every kind of brand: banks, major corporations, large businesses. We have major companies that now handle their financial communications through content creators,” Lesage says, adding that the money from these partnerships goes directly from a company to a content creator without the platform taking a single euro.” The industry’s rapid expansion is also fueling a wave of M&A’s. According to the Paris Creator Week study, 70 acquisitions took place globally in the first half of 2026, up 23% from the same period last year. North America accounted for 64.3% of acquisition targets, compared with 27.1% for Europe. Paris Creator Week is dedicating an entire conference track to M&A, looking at how investors value creator-led businesses and manage the “key man risk,” when companies are built around a single personality. Lesage says some businesses closely tied to their founders have managed to attract investment. For instance, the French podcast company Legend which lured a Belgian fund at a valuation of €72 million. “These are businesses that people thought couldn’t be sold because they were too dependent on a single personality, but we’re seeing that’s not necessarily the case,” he says. For Drew Baldwin, head of Prentiss Media, founder of Tubefilter and creator of the Streamy Awards, the next stage of growth will depend on whether creators can evolve from individual personalities into scalable media businesses. “I still think creators on social platforms, including YouTube, are renting audiences. They don’t own the audience,” Baldwin tells Variety . “And the creators who can figure out how to take their audience and own that relationship are the ones who are going to be able to build new businesses around that community.” Baldwin, who is leading a session comparing the European and American creator economies at the Paris confab, argues France is well positioned to see its local creator economy thrive, even if it’s currently lagging behind the U.S. “France has always been, culturally, a champion of independent voices,” he says. “French cinema has an outsized footprint considering the size of the country. You have the Cannes Film Festival. You have an extraordinary amount of production coming out of France.” “Now, the question is: Will they champion the entrepreneurial spirit? And I think the answer, when I look at Paris Creator Week, is yes.” Baldwin says the U.S. has been ahead of the curve because it’s got a “common language and a more unified advertising market that make it easier to scale businesses.” As in the film and television business, Baldwin anticipates some consolidation in the digital space as creators compete for budgets traditionally reserved for media companies. “Like with any maturation in the economy, there will be consolidation. There will be winners, and there will be those that close shop,” he says. The major challenge is to overcome the key man risk, says Baldwin, who points to MrBeast, Dhar Mann and the British creator collective the Sidemen as examples of creators building businesses capable of expanding beyond their original social media audiences. “Those who can scale, like the Sidemen, WatchTime Studios and Dhar Mann, are the ones who are going to be able to do large-scale media deals,” he says. “Instead of just using creator marketing budgets, they can unlock true media budgets, which are really big.” That convergence is starting to happen even in heavily regulated markets like France, where major production groups including Banijay and Mediawan are exploring opportunities in the creator economy alongside streaming platforms and broadcasters such as TF1, Netflix and Canal+. “Creators are increasingly interested in working with distributors and platforms beyond the ones where they originally built their audiences,” says Lesage-Moretti. “If you’re a YouTuber, it makes sense to be present across social media platforms to diversify, but it also makes sense to explore cinema.” Lesage-Moretti cites the landmark experiment of French YouTuber Inoxtag, whose documentary “Kaizen” was released by MK2 French theaters and sold around 300,000 tickets in a single day. It launched on the same day on YouTube where it generated 40 million or 50 million views overall. Baldwin is also using Paris Creator Week to formally launch Creator Kitchen, an initiative aimed at bringing together executives from traditional and new media. The Paris edition will include an intimate dinner at L’Envol, Michelin-starred chef Thibaut Spiwack’s rooftop restaurant at the Philharmonie de Paris, near the event’s venue. Guests include Twitch CEO Dan Clancy; Justine Ryst, managing director of YouTube France and Southern Europe; Gregg Bywalski, managing director of Webedia Creators; Vincent Grynbaum, managing director of Mediawan Thematics; Nielsen CFO Jessica Holscott; and Mathieu Gallet, managing director of Bourdin Media and chairman of the supervisory board of Les Echos. For Baldwin, the growing appetite for an industry-focused gathering like Paris Creators Week illustrates that the industry is becoming a fully fledged part of the entertainment biz. “Why are thousands of people coming to this? It’s not a fan event. This is the business of the creator economy,” he says. Lesage-Moretti, who is still financing the event with co-founder and managing director Pierre Alary, says they’ve received outside interest but want to keep control. “The real question is what advantage an outside investor would bring us? We have a very clear roadmap and strategy for how we’re going to accelerate our international expansion,” he says. “France has always been able to attract people from all over the world to Cannes for the film festival. We think the same thing should happen in the creator economy.” ‘Yellowjackets’ Season 4 Trailer: The Wilderness Survivors Return Home Loading comments...

title: Jason Sudeikis Takes on Fatherhood, Green Pigs in New ‘Angry Birds Movie 3’ Trailer

title: Stocks Rally Higher After Democrats Flip Congress
full_text: × Breaking News Becerra Wins California Governor; Democrats Take the House and Senate Nov 4, 2026 7:01am PT Stocks Rally Higher After Democrats Flip Congress By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Former OnlyFans Star Camilla Araújo Sets ‘Plot Twist’ Podcast Launch in New Expansion Into Long-Form Entertainment 46 minutes ago Stocks Rally Higher After Democrats Flip Congress 2 hours ago Democrats Win House and Senate in Sweeping Rout of GOP 12 hours ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images Wall Street cheered the Blue Wave that put Democrats in control of both the Senate and House , with major market indexes and media stocks posting gains Wednesday morning after the midterm elections . The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared over 1,100 points in early trading, up 2.2%, to nearly 53,000, while the Nasdaq Composite index was up 2.4%. Analysts said the Democrats’ sweeping congressional win cleared away political uncertainty — and investors were bullish on the likely gridlock in D.C. keeping policies unchanged. Related Stories 'Ellen DeGeneres Show' EP Matthew Wright Dies at 52 in 'Unfathomable Tragedy'; DeGeneres Shares Tearful Video Calling Him the 'Glue to Our Family' “Still more uncertainty looms, but one thing is certain, there will be gridlock and historically this is good for the market,” Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets, told CNBC . Woods said the market uptick also partly stemmed from President Donald Trump’s “initial tone and reaction to the results,” after Trump told the New York Times he would accept the midterm election results . As of Wednesday morning, Democrats held a 54-44 edge in the Senate over Republicans, with two races (in Mississippi and Alaska) yet to be called, according to the AP . In the House, Dems had secured 228 seats — giving the party a clear majority — and the GOP stood at 139, with outcomes in 68 races still undetermined. Media stocks that gained in early trading the morning after the midterms included Netflix (+4%), Comcast (+4%), Disney (+3.8%), Skydance (+2.8%) and Fox Corp. (+2.4%). Big tech stocks — despite analysts warning that Democratic majorities in Congress could create headwinds for AI data center buildouts — also rose: Apple (+6%) Amazon (7.6%), Alphabet (+4.9%) and Meta (+2.4%) all were trending higher. Opposition to massive data center projects became a key issue in the midterms. While some Democratic efforts to curb data center buildouts may be realized, “Our base case is that the data centers are going to be built and delays are already part of life for construction projects,” Jonathan Pingle, chief U.S. economist for UBS, said in a Nov. 4 research note on the elections. “We expect that it may be difficult to come to agreement at the federal level to meaningfully restrain the data center buildout and heavily regulate AI, in particular since the White House has been opposed to doing so.” Not all stocks got a boost. Shares of Elon Musk’s SpaceX were down 1.3% in morning trading and Tesla’s stock was off -2.4%. Musk, the world’s wealthiest individual, spent at least $474 million backing Republican candidates, per CNBC , including $224 million toward the campaign of Texas attorney general Ken Paxton in the contest for the open Senate seat in Texas — which Democrat James Talarico won by a 12-point margin. Voters in Texas also elected Democratic contender Gina Hinojosa governor, who unseated incumbent GOP Gov. Greg Abbott. “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” Musk posted on X late Tuesday night, followed by a shrug emoji. Also falling post-election were shares of Trump Media & Technology Group, the operator of Truth Social (Trump’s primary social media platform). TMTG stock was trading down more than 10% in Wednesday morning trading, pushing its market cap under $1.5 billion. The Trump family trust owns 41% of Trump Media, Reuters reported last month. ‘Yellowjackets’ Season 4 Trailer: The Wilderness Survivors Return Home Loading comments...

title: Thaddea Graham to Be Honored at the Oscar Wilde Awards (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All November 4, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Thaddea Graham Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images for US-Ireland Alliance Thaddea Graham, the actress from Northern Ireland known for her turns on Sex Education at Netflix and Bad Sisters and Margo’s Got Money Troubles at Apple TV, will be honored at the 21st annual Oscar Wilde Awards . Organized by the US-Ireland Alliance, the event is set for March 11 at the Ebell in Los Angeles in its traditional evening spot three days before the Academy Awards. It celebrates the work of those who are Irish — and some who are not — who contribute to film, television and music. Irish American actor Jack Reynor was announced last month as an honoree. Guests also will be treated to a performance by the Irish synth-pop singer Shobsy. Related Stories Movies 'Joy Will Prevail,' Starring Griffin Dunne as Architect Louis Kahn and Alexis Bledel, Tells the Story of the Director's Childhood Home (Exclusive PÖFF Trailer) Movies 'La Bola Negra' Wins Another Prize -- London Film Festival's Audience Award Graham, 29, will receive the Wilde Card Award, “which is presented to someone we expect you’ll hear a lot more from,” US-Ireland Alliance president Trina Vargo said. Previous honorees include Saoirse Ronan, Barry Keoghan, Sarah Bolger and Bad Sisters actress Eve Hewson. Graham last year appeared alongside Julia Roberts, Ayo Edebiri, Andrew Garfield and Michael Stuhlbarg in Luca Guadagnino’s After the Hunt , and she has reunited with the Italian director on the upcoming hot-button film Artificial , which stars Garfield as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. She also played the personal assistant of George Clooney’s actor character in Noah Baumbach’s Jay Kelly (2025). Graham was discovered as a baby on the steps of a building in Changsha, China, when she was a few days old. She was adopted at 13 months and brought by her parents to County Down as one of the first Chinese-born children adopted in Northern Ireland. “I always say I would not be here had it not been for the kindness of strangers,” she told The London Times in April. “From the earliest days of someone stopping and seeing I’d been left, picking me up and looking after me, I’ve seen that kindness throughout my life, from my parents, who are wonderful, through school and the support of my teachers. My primary-school teacher introduced a Chinese New Year celebration, which she continues even though I’m not there anymore.” In 2021, Graham portrayed the head of Sherlock Holmes’ band of street urchins on Netflix’s The Irregulars and recurred on the BBC’s Doctor Who . After playing the therapist O in 2023 on the final season of Sex Education , she sparkled as the stubborn detective Una Houlihan on the second season of Bad Sisters in 2024 and as the roommate of Elle Fanning’s character this year on Margo’s Got Money Troubles . After an FYC Emmy event last year for Bad Sisters , Graham told the Times that she “had a lot of people coming up to me from Asian backgrounds saying, ‘It’s amazing seeing you in this show. It’s amazing seeing you as one of the lead characters. We so admire the kind of representation people are taking over there. And also for you to have a different accent — for you not to have the accent people might expect.’” Shobsy last year completed a U.K. and European tour with SO Recordings labelmates MY BABY, then took the stage at SXSW. In July, he performed at an Irish music industry showcase hosted by Ireland’s president, Catherine Connolly, at her Dublin residence, and he recently released the EP The World Will Not Remember alongside a new single, “Perfect.” Shobsy Courtesy US-Ireland Alliance THR

title: Meta Hires Rich Latour to Lead In-House Content Studio (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All November 4, 2026 6:39am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Rich Latour Courtesy of Subject Meta has hired a TV veteran to lead its in-house content studio. The tech giant and owner of Instagram and Facebook has brought on Rich Latour to be VP of content studio, running its social and content teams within the company’s communications and public affairs division. Latour will report to Tucker Bounds, the company’s head of communications and public affairs, and will be responsible for developing and executing Meta’s content strategy. That will include brand storytelling, focused on the Meta brand and the impact it has on communities; executive social, amplifying brand-level messages through the voices of the company’s top execs; product content support, with a particular emphasis on social; and international social content. Latour joins Meta from BlackRock, where he was managing director, global head of content, creative and events, where he led the investment firm’s global content strategy. Before BlackRock he worked at Goldman Sachs as its VP of digital content. He spent nearly two decades at NBC News, much of it as a producer and senior producer at NBC Nightly News , where he received 4 Emmy Awards and 2 Edward R. Murrow Awards. While Meta’s revenues and profits are still focused within products like Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, Latour joins the as the tech giant is leaning into AI via its Muse agent, and into virtual and augmented reality via its glasses and headsets. While the content studio is outward-facing (it’s about telling Meta’s story), content is poised to become a bigger part of the company’s portfolio. THR

title: ‘Joy Will Prevail,’ Starring Griffin Dunne as Architect Louis Kahn and Alexis Bledel, Tells the Story of the Director’s Childhood Home (Exclusive PÖFF Trailer)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All November 4, 2026 6:01am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Joy Will Prevail' Courtesy of PÖFF Louis I. Kahn , just like the buildings he created, is an architectural icon. The Estonian-born American architect, based in Philadelphia, founded his own atelier in 1935. Among his famous, and often monumental and monolithic, buildings are Bangladesh’s Jatiyo Sangsad Bhaban, or National Assembly Building, the Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth, Texas and the Salk Institute for Biological Studies in La Jolla, California. Now, the final three years of his life and work get the big-screen treatment in Joy Will Prevail , directed by Max Korman, the grandson of Steve Korman, who, as the biographical drama shows, commissioned a house from the celebrated architect outside Philadelphia. The Korman House became the final residential building designed by Kahn. It was completed shortly before his unexpected death in 1974, and it became the director’s childhood home. Related Stories Movies 'La Bola Negra' Wins Another Prize -- London Film Festival's Audience Award Movies Tinie Tempah, Nathalie Emmanuel, Russell Tovey Set for HollyShorts U.K. Honors (Exclusive) Max Korman’s feature debut tells the story of the creation of Kahn’s final residential commission and his unlikely friendship with Steve Korman, painting a portrait of the architect and his legacy. The film also touches on how Kahn quietly navigated a complex personal life as the father of children with three different women. After its recent world premiere at the Philadelphia Film Festival, Joy Will Prevail , appropriately, gets its international premiere in Estonia, at the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival ( PÖFF ), on Saturday, Nov. 7. Griffin Dunne ( The French Dispatch , After Hours , An American Werewolf in London ) stars as Louis I. Kahn, with Jennifer Beals ( The L Word , NCIS: New York , Flashdance ) and Alexis Bledel ( The Handmaid’s Tale , Gilmore Girls ) adding further star power. Ben Rosenfield portrays Steve Korman, with Molly Ephraim also part of the ensemble cast. Joshua Echevarria was the cinematographer, with editing handled by Sarah Flack. J. Andrew Greenblatt, Max Korman, Derek Dienner and Alex Peace-Power are the producers on Joy Will Prevail , with co-producers Anthony Faure, Christopher Rivera and Grace Wagner. Kahn, born in Kuressaare on the Estonian island of Saaremaa, and the story of his final years return to the country where his life began this weekend. After the Saturday PÖFF premiere in the presence of Dunne and director Korman, the film team will visit Kuressaare for a special Sunday screening of Joy Will Prevail . Their visit to Estonia is organized in cooperation with the Louis Kahn Estonia Foundation. THR can now exclusively premiere a trailer for the film. It provides a first appetizer for the biographical and cinematic journey that is Joy Will Prevail . Watch the teaser with Dunne, Beals, Bledel and more right here. THR
